strengths: Relevant and practical problem: open-domain tabular QA retrieval with a training-free cascade using off-the-shelf models, addressing retraining cost and adaptability.

Comprehensive empirical study on NQ-Tables, including multiple sparse/dense/hybrid baselines, stage-wise ablations, query decomposition/table description/row filtering analyses, perturbation robustness, token-efficiency, and end-to-end QA with several LLMs.

Results show clear gains at deeper retrieval ranks (R@10/R@50), strong robustness under query paraphrasing relative to DTR, substantial token reduction from sub-table context, and competitive end-to-end F1 with larger LLMs.
weaknesses: Retrieval evaluation may conflate mini-tables and tables. The pipeline ranks row-level mini-tables in later stages, but it is not clearly described how these are mapped/deduplicated to table-level R@K for comparison with table-retrieval baselines; if mini-tables are counted as separate items, reported recall may be inflated and not comparable.

Central claim is overstated: abstract says CRAFT achieves better retrieval performance than SOTA sparse/dense/hybrid retrievers, but Table 1 shows CRAFT is worse at R@1 than THYME, BIBERT+SPLADE, T-RAG*, and DTR variants; it only edges ahead at R@10/R@50. The paper should qualify this as a deeper-recall trade-off.

Reproducibility is limited: several components are proprietary (Gemini 1.5 Flash/2.5 Flash, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small), decoding/version details are missing, no code/data or generated descriptions/subquestions are released, and no significance testing is provided. Evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (NQ-Tables), despite claims of general open-domain TQA.

Technical novelty is modest: the method is essentially a pipeline of existing sparse/dense embedding models plus LLM preprocessing, and the 'neural reranker' is embedding similarity rather than a cross-encoder. The contribution would benefit from stronger baselines, more datasets, and clearer isolation of the benefits of each LLM-generated component (e.g., table descriptions did not help SPLADE in Table 6).

End-to-end comparisons are not fully controlled: it is unclear whether baseline RAG/DPR-RAGE/LI-RAGE results use the same LLMs, prompts, and retrieval depth, and few-shot gains are inconsistent across models in Table 12, weakening the strength of the conclusion.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem—training-free, open-domain table retrieval—and proposes a clear, modular three-stage cascade (sparse SPLADE filtering, dense mpnet reranking, neural re-ranking with text-embedding-3-small) whose design is easy to follow.

The stage-wise ablations (Tables 5, 6, 8, 9, 10) are informative and cleanly attribute gains to each component: table descriptions help BM25 but not SPLADE, query decomposition helps both, and the dense and neural stages progressively sharpen ranking. This decomposition supports the design rationale.

The robustness experiment under query paraphrasing (Table 2) is a valuable and relatively uncommon analysis, showing that CRAFT degrades far less than fine-tuned DTR variants under perturbation—an argument for the modular, training-free approach.
The token-consumption analysis (Table 13) showing ~70% context reduction with sub-table inputs is a practically useful efficiency result that supports deployment claims.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: full prompts are provided (Figures 2–4), model names are specified, and training/inference configuration is reported (Table 11).
The end-to-end evaluation spans three open LLMs (Mistral-7B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) and multiple retrieval depths (n = 1, 3, 5, 8, 10), giving a reasonably broad view of downstream behavior.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. The abstract and introduction state that CRAFT achieves "better retrieval performance than state-of-the-art (SOTA) sparse, dense, and hybrid retrievers," but Table 1 shows CRAFT substantially trailing THYME at R@1 (41.13 vs 48.55), the most decision-relevant retrieval metric, and losing to DTR(M)+HN at R@1 as well (47.33). The gains are confined to R@10/R@50, and this limitation is only mentioned in passing.

The "training-free" framing is somewhat misleading. Preprocessing and query expansion rely on Gemini 1.5 Flash, a very large proprietary LLM, so the method offloads substantial computation and knowledge to a stronger model rather than eliminating it. This weakens the fairness of comparisons against models fine-tuned only on NQ-Tables and undermines the implied cost/adaptability advantage.

Evaluation is restricted to a single benchmark (NQ-Tables), which the authors acknowledge in Limitations but which materially limits the generalizability claims. No variance estimates, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere, despite several margins being small (e.g., CRAFT vs THYME at R@50).

The end-to-end comparisons do not appear fully apples-to-apples. Table 4 reports results with Mistral-Small-Instruct, which is likely a much larger model than the 7B-class models used in Table 3, so the comparison against LI-RAGE/DPR-RAGE/TABERT may conflate retriever quality with model scale. It is also unclear whether the baseline retriever+LLM numbers in Table 3 were recomputed by the authors under identical prompts or borrowed from prior work.

Technical novelty is modest: the framework composes off-the-shelf components (SPLADE, mpnet, text-embedding-3-small, Gemini) into a cascade, and the contribution is largely engineering integration plus descriptive analysis rather than a new method or insight.

Reproducibility is partially compromised by dependence on proprietary, versioned APIs (Gemini 1.5 Flash, text-embedding-3-small), whose behavior can drift; no seeds or variance reporting are provided to gauge stability of the reported numbers.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: open-domain table question answering, where retrieval from large table corpora remains difficult.
Proposes a modular, training-free cascaded retrieval pipeline that combines sparse retrieval, dense semantic reranking, and neural reranking without dataset-specific fine-tuning.
Provides some reproducibility effort by listing models used and including the key prompts for answer generation, table description, and query expansion in the appendix.
Evaluates robustness under query paraphrasing and shows CRAFT recovers more gracefully than DTR baselines on the perturbed-query setting.

Includes useful ablation analyses over stages, table descriptions, query decomposition, and irrelevant-context reduction, as well as token-consumption comparisons for sub-table vs. full-table contexts.
Shows strong recall at R@10 and R@50 on NQ-Tables and reports end-to-end F1 results across several LLMs and retrieval depths.
weaknesses: The central retrieval claim is overstated: CRAFT achieves lower R@1 (41.13) than THYME (48.55), T-RAG* (46.07), SSDR(im) (45.47), and BIBERT+SPLADE (45.62). It is only better at R@10/R@50, so the abstract claim that it achieves 'better retrieval performance than state-of-the-art sparse, dense, and hybrid retrievers' is not supported.

The end-to-end claim that CRAFT 'outperforms all existing TQA-in-the-wild' is not adequately supported. The text states Mistral-Small-Instruct achieves 50.26 F1 and 'already surpassing the best-performing baseline, LI-RAGE (54.17)', but 50.26 < 54.17. It only surpasses LI-RAGE at n=5, and the comparison uses different LLM sizes, retrieval depths, and possibly different evaluation metrics.

Results are internally inconsistent. Table 3 reports CRAFT (5-fewshot) lower than zero-shot CRAFT for Llama3 at n=3 (39.39 vs. 44.06) and n=5 (39.27 vs. 45.98), contradicting the text's claim that few-shot prompting 'enhances performance substantially across all models and top-k tables.'

The comparison with prior dataset-specific baselines is not controlled. CRAFT uses stronger off-the-shelf embedding models and proprietary Gemini 1.5 Flash for table descriptions and query expansion, while prior work may use different LLMs, prompts, retrieval depths, and metrics, making direct F1 comparisons unreliable.

The 'training-free' framing hides substantial preprocessing cost and reliance on proprietary models. Generating titles and descriptions for 169,898 tables with Gemini 1.5 Flash is expensive, and error propagation from these generated descriptions and sub-questions is not analyzed.
No statistical significance testing or error bars are provided. The NQ-Tables test set has only 919 unique queries, and several reported improvements are small enough that they may be noise.

Reproducibility is limited. Key details are missing, including exact SPLADE version/configuration, Gemini and text-embedding-3-small snapshots, random seeds, preprocessing costs, and full implementation settings for the CRAFT pipeline. The training configuration table is for baselines, not CRAFT.

Novelty is limited. Cascaded retrieval and reranking with off-the-shelf models is a straightforward engineering pipeline; using an LLM to generate table descriptions and sub-questions is incremental rather than a new method or insight.

The evaluation metric for end-to-end QA is F1, but it is unclear whether prior baselines report the same metric or exact match/accuracy. Direct comparisons to LI-RAGE, RAG, and DPR-RAGE may therefore be invalid.

Important analyses are missing. There is no end-to-end comparison against THYME despite it being a strong retrieval baseline, no detailed error analysis for CRAFT's lower R@1, and no evaluation of the full CRAFT pipeline with larger LLMs across all retrieval depths.

The limitations section is too brief and does not acknowledge the overclaiming, metric mismatches, or comparison problems. The paper would require substantial revisions to align its claims with the actual evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically important problem: open-domain table retrieval for tabular QA, where scalable retrieval remains a bottleneck. The proposed CRAFT cascade is a sensible, modular design combining sparse retrieval, dense pruning, and neural reranking without dataset-specific fine-tuning.

The empirical evaluation is broad: two benchmarks (NQ-Tables and OTT-QA), many retrieval baselines, multiple LLMs, end-to-end QA evaluation, robustness to query paraphrasing, efficiency analysis, and ablations. This gives reasonable evidence for the main claims.

The results support the retrieval claims: CRAFT achieves strong retrieval recall on NQ-Tables, with especially high R@50 (97.17), and is competitive on OTT-QA at higher recall thresholds (e.g., R@10 89.88, R@50 96.07) despite being training-free.

The ablation studies are useful and reasonably clear. They show the contribution of generated table descriptions, query decomposition, irrelevant-row filtering, and neural reranking, strengthening confidence in the pipeline design.

The efficiency analysis is a practical strength: mini-table construction reduces token usage by over 70% and pruning reduces online embedding calls by roughly 33x, while maintaining high Stage-1 recall. This makes the approach attractive for real-world deployment.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear figures and tables, and it includes prompts and hyperparameter details. The limitations section and ethics statement are appropriately candid.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code/data link: the abstract says "Code and data are available at:" but no actual URL is provided. Several implementation details are also under-specified, including the exact row-ranking procedure, how mini-table embeddings are formed, and the precise values of K/N1/N2/N3 in the cascade.

The comparison is not fully controlled. CRAFT benefits from LLM-generated table descriptions and query expansions, while many baselines operate on raw tables and queries. Although this is part of the method, it makes the retrieval and end-to-end comparisons less apples-to-apples than the paper often implies.

Some central claims are overstated. On OTT-QA, CRAFT's R@1 (55.56) is substantially below THYME (66.67), so calling the zero-shot performance "competitive" is fair mainly at higher recall cutoffs, not at top-1. The end-to-end OTT-QA results are oracle settings with gold passages, not a full open-domain pipeline.

The comparison to LI-RAGE in Table 6 is acknowledged as not directly comparable, yet it is still used to support a "current SOTA" claim. This should be framed much more cautiously, as the setups and baselines differ.

Novelty is moderate: the system largely combines existing components (SPLADE, dense bi-encoders, off-the-shelf embedding models, LLM-generated table descriptions, and cascaded retrieval). The contribution is primarily engineering/integration rather than a new retrieval paradigm.

There are no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals, and some results are close enough that significance is unclear. The robustness analysis is limited to DTR as a baseline and mostly to NQ-Tables.

A few details are internally inconsistent or confusing: for example, Table 8 uses boxed values to indicate tables passed to the next stage, but the text describes Stage 2 as passing 5,000 tables and Stage 3 as reranking the top 100, which does not fully align. More precise notation and stage-wise counts would improve clarity.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: open-domain table QA with a training-free, modular, and adaptable retrieval pipeline that avoids dataset-specific fine-tuning.
The multi-stage cascade is well motivated and the stage-wise ablations (Tables 8-12) clearly show how each component contributes to retrieval performance.
Extensive empirical evaluation on two benchmarks, NQ-Tables and OTT-QA, with multiple sparse, dense, and hybrid baselines, plus end-to-end QA experiments with several LLMs.
Strong retrieval results on NQ-Tables: CRAFT achieves 49.84 R@1, 86.83 R@10, and 97.17 R@50, outperforming competitive baselines including THYME and DTR variants.
The use of LLM-generated table titles/descriptions and query decomposition is supported by ablations (Tables 9-10), demonstrating consistent gains from enriched representations.
The mini-table representation is well analyzed, with Table 7 showing >70% token reduction and the efficiency section claiming up to 33x fewer online embedding calls without major accuracy loss.
Robustness to query paraphrasing is evaluated against DTR, and the cascade is shown to recover much of the degraded recall across stages (Table 4).
The paper includes useful error analysis and case studies (Tables 16-17) illustrating when full-table context fails and mini-table denoising helps.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the paper combines existing ideas (sparse+dense cascade, LLM-based query/table augmentation, mini-table filtering) and mainly offers an empirical system contribution rather than a new retrieval method.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code/data link in the abstract ('Code and data are available at:' with no URL) and heavy reliance on proprietary, versioned APIs such as Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini embeddings, OpenAI text-embedding-3, and GPT-4o.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. On NQ-Tables, CRAFT uses LLM-generated descriptions and multiple embedding models while some baselines are fine-tuned; preprocessing and API costs are not compared fairly. End-to-end Table 6 compares against prior baselines that may use different LLM readers.

On OTT-QA, CRAFT trails fine-tuned hybrid retrievers substantially at R@1 (55.56 vs. 66.67 for THYME), so the 'competitive' claim holds mainly at higher recall thresholds (R@10/R@50), not at top-rank retrieval.
The OTT-QA end-to-end evaluation uses an oracle setting with gold passages, not a full open-domain retrieval pipeline, which limits the strength of the end-to-end open-domain QA claim.

Efficiency claims are supported by token counts and embedding-call counts, but not by wall-clock latency or monetary/API cost. The training-free pipeline still requires expensive offline precomputation and per-query LLM calls for query expansion.
Experimental rigor could be improved: no variance estimates or statistical significance tests are reported, and some split/subset details for NQ-Tables and OTT-QA are not fully specified.

The Stage 3 configuration is inconsistent across tables: the best NQ-Tables result uses text-embedding-3-large while the main stage-wise table uses text-embedding-3-small, making the headline 'CRAFT' result harder to interpret.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: open-domain table QA retrieval with a modular, multi-stage retrieval pipeline.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation on two benchmarks (NQ-Tables and OTT-QA), with comparisons to a wide range of sparse, dense, and hybrid retrievers.
Includes useful component ablations: generated table descriptions, query decomposition, dense semantic pruning, neural reranking, and mini-table context construction.
The mini-table representation is practically valuable: it reduces token/context length by over 70% and yields qualitative case studies where full-table context causes failure or hallucination.
Demonstrates better robustness than DTR under query paraphrasing and provides prompt templates in the appendix to aid some reproducibility.
Reports strong retrieval results on NQ-Tables, achieving top R@1 and high R@50, and provides end-to-end QA results with multiple LLMs.
weaknesses: The central "training-free/zero-shot" framing is overstated. The method depends heavily on Gemini-generated table descriptions, query decomposition, and perturbation, plus dataset-specific choices of embedding models and rerankers, so it is not truly training-free or fully zero-shot in a broad sense.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript says "Code and data are available at:" but no URL is visible; the pipeline relies on proprietary Gemini and OpenAI models whose versions and outputs may change; no multiple runs, variance estimates, or statistical significance tests are reported.

The OTT-QA evaluation is not fully open-domain: end-to-end QA uses an oracle setting with gold passages, and retrieval R@1 (55.56) is substantially below supervised SPLADE (62.74), while R@10/R@50 are below THYME and BIBERT+SPLADE. The claim of "strong zero-shot performance" is therefore overstated.

Several gains are small and may not be reliable: e.g., NQ-Tables R@1 improves over THYME by 1.29 points and R@10 over BIBERT+SPLADE by only 0.11 points, with no confidence intervals or significance testing on a 966-query test set.

End-to-end comparisons may be confounded: CRAFT uses mini-table contexts while some baselines likely use full-table contexts, so gains could reflect context construction rather than retrieval quality. A controlled apples-to-apples comparison is missing.

Potential benchmark contamination is not discussed. Gemini is used to generate table descriptions and sub-questions for benchmark instances; if Gemini has seen these public benchmarks during pretraining, the retrieval evaluation may be partially contaminated by external knowledge.
Novelty is modest: cascaded sparse-dense-rerank pipelines and LLM-generated table/query representations are established ideas. The contribution is mostly engineering with limited conceptual advance.

Some methodological details are unclear: the preprocessing row-ranking step, how mini-tables are formed and scored, how K values are chosen, and the exact prompts/hyperparameters used for CRAFT are not fully specified in the main paper.

Efficiency claims are not fully supported. Stage 2 still performs 5,100 mini-table embeddings per query online, and the offline cost of running Gemini over 169K/419K tables is not analyzed; the "33x fewer online embedding calls" claim may obscure overall computational cost.
